The economics aren't that simple. Depending on which model you use the number of firms required to hit market prices can be as low as two depending on the setup of the market (essentially how easy is it to scale production). While monopolistic competition is a valid theory within limited frameworks it likely isn't here as there are many substitutes to shopping online unless you live in a rural area. If Amazon were to dramatically increase prices their business would likely loose a good chunk of people that can go to the only slightly more expensive brick and mortar operations for non-emergent goods. In fact Amazon is focusing on reducing delivery times by using drones in test markets to prevent this very phenomenon and create a niche market (when you need it right now). While it's likely that in rural areas they can effectively charge whatever they want because people may simply lack local options, in urban environments increased prices can drive people back to the brick and mortars or open up room for other online retailers. It is worth noting that Amazon started as a book retailer which is an industry with notoriously high inventory costs even though books themselves are not that expensive. By nationalizing the market and going online they could offer more titles than their competitors. Their general marketing strategy is fairly similar. Have everything and be able to offer it for less because they are selling to a larger market thus reducing inventory costs.

TL;DR Even if they have the internet cornered they still compete with local retailers.
